sources.title: PSI record PSI-26: Burning and Suppression of Solids
sources.label: BASS
sources.text:
Investigation: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS)
Accession: PSI-26. DOI: 10.60555/58h4-dy80.
Project type: Microgravity Investigation. Flight program: International Space Station (ISS).
Dates: 10-01-2009 to 06-30-2013.
Hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox.
Objective: The two main objectives for BASS are to: 1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible). 2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.
Hypothesis: BASS experiments were based on the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.) To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft.
Approach: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction. This investigation explored two primary air flow configurations; concurrent-flow and opposed-flow. With concurrent-flow air flows in the same direction as the flame spread and in opposed-flow air flows in the opposite direction of flame spread. Flames were observed in the top and edge profiles and data was collected on flame size, shape, color, spread rate, and potential flame quenching. The samples were placed in a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) that allowed for airflow across the fabric. Other sample shapes were utilized as well including spheres and cylinders.
Research impacts: Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects. A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame. These results are used in first order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and as a means to extend heat release data from tests like the NASA cone calorimeter test (NASA–STD–6001 Test 2) to a performance-based material selection process. Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques. BASS results provide essential guidance to ground-based microgravity combustion research efforts. Detailed combustion models are validated using the simpler flow environment afforded by tests in microgravity. Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity. These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems and will guide novel spacecraft design and ensure the safety of future crewed missions.

sources.text: PSI Data Layout Document – BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids) Investigation BASS (Burning and Suppression of Solids) examines the burning and extinction characteristics of a wide variety of fuel samples in microgravity. The BASS experiment will guide strategies for extinguishing accidental fires in microgravity. BASS results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth. sources.title: PSI-26_Presentations_Crew Training 2010.pdf, page 3 (BASS)
sources.label: BASS
sources.text: INTRODUCTION • Three investigations will be performed: SPICE, SLICE, and BASS. • These investigations will be performed inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG). • SPICE is based on the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) hardware which flew on STS-87 in 1997. • SPICE hardware is already on-orbit. It has successfully completed all of its objectives with the collection of 200 data points in the first half of 2009. Spare gas onboard will now be used to collect additional data. New fuel is being flown on ULF5 to support the SLICE and BASS experiments. • SPICE hardware will also be used to perform SLICE and BASS. • SPICE burns different fuels to investigate the point at which they begin to smoke. • SLICE burns different fuels to investigate the structure of flames when lifted from the fuel nozzle. • BASS burns different materials to investigate how they burn in microgravity.
